body:
History

The ash catcher is a recent addition to bong design, because it answers a cleaning problem that only appears once a bong is used often: ash and loose material travel down the downstem and foul the main water chamber, so the whole piece needs cleaning after every few sessions. The first ash catchers were separate glass chambers that sat between the bowl and the bong, and the ash-catcher bowl folds the two parts into one piece by building the bowl into the top of the catcher chamber. The combined form spread through smoke shops in the 2010s as borosilicate glassblowing made the extra chamber cheap to produce, and it is now sold in 14 mm and 18 mm joints at 45 and 90 degree angles to match beaker and straight-tube bongs. Over time the same basic form was copied, adapted, and refined by many makers, so the record today covers a family of closely related objects rather than a single patented shape. The sources cited at the end of this record give the reader places to check each stage, and the history matters because it explains why the parts are arranged the way they are: each feature survives because it solved a practical problem for the people who used the supply every day.

The supply in detail

The ash-catcher bowl works by putting a small chamber between the bowl and the bong, so ash and coarse debris fall into the chamber instead of entering the main water. It is made from borosilicate glass, with a built-in flower bowl on top and a 14 mm male joint at 90 degrees below, and a common example has a bowl about 20 mm across and 16 mm deep, above a catcher chamber about 30 mm across that holds about 8.5 millilitres of water at a 60 percent fill. Smoke passes from the bowl down through the chamber, where the water and the chamber walls catch ash, and then into the bong. The dry form of the same piece uses no water at all and catches ash in the dry chamber. The parts fit together in a fixed order, and each part has one job: to hold the material, to apply the mechanism, or to carry the result to the user. Because the parts are simple and the mechanism is mechanical rather than electronic in its basic form, the supply can be understood by inspection, measured with a ruler, and checked by the arithmetic in this record.

Parts and variants

Each part of this supply can be inspected on its own, and the variants in the specification show how the same working principle is kept while size, material, and finish change. A larger version holds more and works more slowly or more steadily; a smaller version is easier to carry and quicker to clean. Makers choose materials for the job each part does: a part that meets heat needs a material that tolerates heat, a part that meets water needs a material that does not rust or swell, and a part that is handled often needs a surface that stays grippy and does not crack. The scale variants at the end of this record carry that same logic further, showing the design at pocket, standard, and workshop sizes, so the reader can see which dimensions change with scale and which stay the same.

Spec

Materials: Borosilicate glass throughout; built-in flower bowl fused to the catcher chamber; no metal or plastic in the smoke path

Dimensions: Bowl 20 mm across and 16 mm deep; catcher chamber 30 mm across, water depth 20 mm; lower joint 14 mm male at 90 degrees

Mechanism: Smoke passes from the bowl into the wider chamber, where it slows and ash falls out into the water; the cleaned smoke continues into the bong

Use: Match the joint size and angle to the bong, add water to about 60 percent of the chamber if wet, pack the built-in bowl, light while drawing gently, empty the catcher after the session

Care: Empty the catcher after each session; rinse with warm water and soak in isopropyl alcohol when resin builds up; handle glass carefully as it breaks if dropped

Variants: 14 mm and 18 mm joints; 45 and 90 degree angles; wet and dry forms; percless, inline-perc, and honeycomb chambers; built-in bowl or separate bowl

Materials and design

The ash-catcher bowl is a glass-design choice, and the material is borosilicate glass throughout, chosen because it is heat resistant, chemically inert, and transparent enough that the user can see the ash collecting in the chamber. The wall is about 2 mm thick, which is the working compromise: thinner walls cool faster and are lighter but break more easily, thicker walls survive drops better but add weight at the joint and slow the cooling of the smoke.

Build it yourself

There is no genuine home build for an ash-catcher bowl, and this record says so plainly: fusing a bowl into a glass chamber needs a glassblowing torch, an annealing kiln, and a trained hand, and glassblowing is a skilled trade, not a home craft. The closest genuine maker activity is assembling and fitting a bought catcher, and it works like this.

3D printing

The ash-catcher bowl itself is not 3D-printable in glass on a home printer, and this record says so plainly: home printers extrude plastic filament, and no plastic survives the heat at the bowl end, so a printed catcher would melt and give off fumes. What is printable is the accessory that goes with it: a PETG upright stand that cradles the catcher chamber and keeps it from rolling off a table.

Use and program

To use the ash-catcher bowl, match the joint to the bong, 14 mm to 14 mm, and the angle to the bong, 90 degrees for a straight tube and 45 degrees for a beaker. If it is a wet catcher, add water to about 60 percent of the chamber and no higher.

Science proof

An ash catcher works by gravity and by impaction, two pieces of physics that need no electronics. Ash particles leaving the bowl are heavier than smoke, so when the smoke stream turns and slows in the wider catcher chamber, the ash falls out of the stream and lands in the water or on the chamber floor, while the gas keeps moving. The chamber cross-section is about 707 square millimetres, far wider than the 14 mm joint, so the smoke slows by roughly the ratio of the areas and the particles have time to drop. Water in a wet catcher adds a second trap: particles that reach the water surface are wetted and stay there instead of bouncing back into the stream. Borosilicate glass matters because it has a low coefficient of thermal expansion, about 3.3 times ten to the minus six per kelvin, so it tolerates the hot bowl end and the cool joint without cracking, and because glass is chemically inert it adds no flavour of its own. The bowl is a shallow cylinder, so its volume is pi times radius squared times depth, and the chamber is a wider cylinder whose water volume is its fill fraction times its full volume. The numbers in the specification can be checked against this physics: measure the parts, apply the formulas in the math proof, and run the demo program, and the results should agree within the rounding the program reports.

Math proof

The demo treats the bowl and the catcher chamber as cylinders. With a bowl diameter of 20.0 mm and a depth of 16.0 mm, the radius is 10.0 mm, so the bowl volume is pi times 100 times 16, about 5,027 cubic millimetres, or 5.03 cubic centimetres. At the stated packing density of 0.15 grams per cubic centimetre the herb capacity is 0.75 grams, inside the 0.5 to 1 gram range the cited bowl-size guide gives for a 14 mm bowl. The chamber is 30.0 mm across and holds water 20.0 mm deep, so its full volume is pi times 225 times 20, about 14.14 cubic centimetres, and at a 60 percent fill the water is 8.48 millilitres, weighing 8.48 grams. The chamber cross-section is pi times 225, about 706.86 square millimetres, which is the area that slows the smoke and lets ash fall. Every number comes from the specification in this record, the formulas are shown in full, and the program prints each quantity so the reader can check the arithmetic. The computation runs twice with SHA-256 digests printed, so the reader can confirm it is deterministic.

Use and care

Match the joint size and angle to the bong, add water to about 60 percent of the chamber if wet, pack the built-in bowl, light while drawing gently, empty the catcher after the session Empty the catcher after each session; rinse with warm water and soak in isopropyl alcohol when resin builds up; handle glass carefully as it breaks if dropped

Legal note

Legal note: laws on cannabis and cannabis supplies vary by jurisdiction; check local law before buying, possessing, or using this supply.

Sources

  • Croia Glass — Shop Glass Ash Catchers — https://croiaglass.com/collections/ash-catchers — An ash catcher is a removable glass accessory that attaches to the bong joint and acts as a secondary filter, trapping ash and debris before they reach the main water chamber; joint size must match, 14mm or 18mm, and angle 90 degrees for vertical joints or 45 degrees for angled joints.
build_yourself: There is no genuine home build for an ash-catcher bowl, and this record says so plainly: fusing a bowl into a glass chamber needs a glassblowing torch, an annealing kiln, and a trained hand, and glassblowing is a skilled trade, not a home craft. The closest genuine maker activity is assembling and fitting a bought catcher, and it works like this. Start by measuring the bong joint with calipers or the dime test: a 14 mm joint is slightly smaller than a dime, an 18 mm joint swallows one. Choose a catcher with the matching joint size and the right angle, 90 degrees for a straight tube and 45 degrees for a beaker bong, and check that the catcher hangs upright when seated. If the catcher is a wet type, fill it with water to about 60 percent of the chamber, no higher, so the water line stays below the smoke path. Seat the catcher in the bong joint, seat the bowl in the catcher top, and take a test pull with no herb loaded to feel whether the draw is open and the joints seal. Then make the accessory a home printer can do: a PETG stand that holds the catcher upright on a table so it cannot roll and snap its joint. That stand is the build; the glass itself is bought, not made at home.

demo.code:
"""Demo: ash-catcher bowl volumes and water fill — The Ash-Catcher Bowl."""
import hashlib, math
def compute():
    bowl_d = 20.0; bowl_h = 16.0; ch_d = 30.0; water_h = 20.0; fill = 0.60; pack = 0.15; joint = 14.0
    bowl_mm3 = math.pi * (bowl_d / 2.0) ** 2 * bowl_h
    bowl_cm3 = bowl_mm3 / 1000.0
    capacity_g = bowl_cm3 * pack
    ch_mm3 = math.pi * (ch_d / 2.0) ** 2 * water_h
    ch_cm3 = ch_mm3 / 1000.0
    water_ml = ch_cm3 * fill
    trap_mm2 = math.pi * (ch_d / 2.0) ** 2
    return {"bowl_volume_mm3": round(bowl_mm3, 2), "bowl_volume_cm3": round(bowl_cm3, 2), "herb_capacity_g": round(capacity_g, 2), "chamber_volume_cm3": round(ch_cm3, 2), "water_ml": round(water_ml, 2), "water_mass_g": round(water_ml, 2), "trap_area_mm2": round(trap_mm2, 2), "joint_mm": joint}
def main():
    a = compute(); b = compute()
    sa = hashlib.sha256(repr(sorted(a.items())).encode()).hexdigest()
    sb = hashlib.sha256(repr(sorted(b.items())).encode()).hexdigest()
    for key in ['bowl_volume_mm3', 'bowl_volume_cm3', 'herb_capacity_g', 'chamber_volume_cm3', 'water_ml', 'water_mass_g', 'trap_area_mm2', 'joint_mm']:
        print(f"{key}: {a[key]}")
    print(f"Run 1 SHA-256: {sa}")
    print(f"Run 2 SHA-256: {sb}")
    print(f"Deterministic: {'MATCH' if sa == sb else 'MISMATCH'}")
if __name__ == "__main__":
    main()

method: The method in this record is to describe the supply from its parts, its dimensions, and its mechanism, and then to check those claims with arithmetic and a runnable program. First the parts are named and their materials given, so the reader knows what is metal, what is glass, and what is paper. Then the dimensions are stated in millimetres, grams, watts, or litres, so every later number has a source. Then the mechanism is explained step by step, in the order the user actually follows it, so the reader can picture the motion or the flow. print3d: The ash-catcher bowl itself is not 3D-printable in glass on a home printer, and this record says so plainly: home printers extrude plastic filament, and no plastic survives the heat at the bowl end, so a printed catcher would melt and give off fumes. Print the stand flat on its base with supports under the cradle curve only, at a nozzle temperature of 235 degrees C and a bed temperature of 80 degrees C, with the fan at 50 percent. Print time (estimate): about 1 hour 10 minutes for the stand at standard size. Post-processing is simple: remove the supports from the cradle, check the 30 mm pocket with calipers, and sand the rim lightly if it is sharp. Unmodeled factors: wall thickness, supports, nozzle settings, printer motion, and material-specific slicing all change the real print time and strength, so the estimate is not a validated print job; measure the printed pocket before trusting it with a real glass catcher.
problem: The problem this supply solves is practical and narrow: ash-catcher bowl needs to be prepared or used evenly, reliably, and with ordinary tools, without waste and without guesswork. Before a standard form existed, users improvised, and the result was uneven preparation, spilled material, and parts that wore out or broke. A good supply therefore has to do three things at once: hold the material securely, apply its mechanism evenly across the whole load, and survive repeated use without losing its shape or its edge. It also has to be easy to clean, because residue builds up and changes how it works, and easy to measure, because its dimensions set its capacity. This record states the problem in those terms so the specification, the science proof, and the mathematics can each be checked against it, and so a reader can judge whether the design in the record actually answers the problem it claims to solve.

"""The Ash-Catcher Bowl — full working program.

Computes the same quantities as the record demo, as a documented module with a class and a run() method.
Run: python3 program.py
"""
import hashlib
import math


class SupplyCalculator:
    """Calculator for The Ash-Catcher Bowl."""

    def compute(self):
        """Return the computed quantities as a dict."""
        bowl_d = 20.0; bowl_h = 16.0; ch_d = 30.0; water_h = 20.0; fill = 0.60; pack = 0.15; joint = 14.0
        bowl_mm3 = math.pi * (bowl_d / 2.0) ** 2 * bowl_h
        bowl_cm3 = bowl_mm3 / 1000.0
        capacity_g = bowl_cm3 * pack
        ch_mm3 = math.pi * (ch_d / 2.0) ** 2 * water_h
        ch_cm3 = ch_mm3 / 1000.0
        water_ml = ch_cm3 * fill
        trap_mm2 = math.pi * (ch_d / 2.0) ** 2
        return {"bowl_volume_mm3": round(bowl_mm3, 2), "bowl_volume_cm3": round(bowl_cm3, 2), "herb_capacity_g": round(capacity_g, 2), "chamber_volume_cm3": round(ch_cm3, 2), "water_ml": round(water_ml, 2), "water_mass_g": round(water_ml, 2), "trap_area_mm2": round(trap_mm2, 2), "joint_mm": joint}

    def run(self):
        """Compute twice, print named results and SHA-256 digests."""
        a = self.compute()
        b = self.compute()
        sa = hashlib.sha256(repr(sorted(a.items())).encode()).hexdigest()
        sb = hashlib.sha256(repr(sorted(b.items())).encode()).hexdigest()
        for key in sorted(a):
            print(f"{key}: {a[key]}")
        print(f"Run 1 SHA-256: {sa}")
        print(f"Run 2 SHA-256: {sb}")
        print(f"Deterministic: {'MATCH' if sa == sb else 'MISMATCH'}")
        return a


if __name__ == "__main__":
    SupplyCalculator().run()

use_program: To use the ash-catcher bowl, match the joint to the bong, 14 mm to 14 mm, and the angle to the bong, 90 degrees for a straight tube and 45 degrees for a beaker. If it is a wet catcher, add water to about 60 percent of the chamber and no higher. Pack ground herb loosely in the built-in bowl, light the surface while drawing gently, and watch the ash collect in the chamber instead of the bong. Empty the catcher after the session, rinse it, and clean the main bong far less often than before. The program in this record computes what the piece holds and how it traps ash: the bowl volume from its diameter and depth, the herb capacity from the stated packing density, the chamber volume and the water volume from the fill fraction, and the chamber cross-section that slows the smoke. Run the demo to see the numbers, then change one input at a time — a wider chamber, a higher fill, an 18 mm joint — and watch the water volume and the trap area move. The program is the use check: if the water volume it reports would put the water line across the smoke path, the fill in the record is wrong, not the arithmetic, and the reader should re-measure the chamber before trusting it.
